Well, hi Doctor. I suppose I'm here because of my job. I work as a cashier, and, well, things have been getting really complicated for me at the register lately. It’s a bit hard to explain, but I keep getting... stuck, I guess you could say. 

I'll be in the middle of ringing someone up—just a normal transaction, maybe they have a few items, some groceries, nothing out of the ordinary—and suddenly I find myself doing these things that just really don’t fit the moment at all. For example, I’ll start tapping the barcode scanner on the edge of the counter in this very specific pattern, just tap-tap-tapping it, instead of actually scanning the next item. I don't really know why, it's just what happens. 

Or, and this is what really caused a major problem the other day, I'll just freeze completely. I had the cash drawer pop open after I totaled the order, and my hand was just hovering right there over the bills, and I just froze. I couldn't move it. The customer was standing right in front of me, just waiting for their change, shifting from foot to foot, looking at me like I was crazy, and I was just stuck there with my hand in the air over the drawer. It's so frustrating because I know they're waiting, and I know how to do my job—I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, the math is certainly not the issue—but I just get caught in these moments where my body just stops or repeats things. 

And because of all that, my manager actually pulled me aside into the back office last week and I got written up. They had the whole official form and everything, talking about productivity and customer complaints, and it's just... it's really stressful because I need to keep this job, you know? So I figured I had to come in and see if someone could help me figure out why I keep getting stuck like that.

Well, that's the thing, Doctor, and it's what makes the whole situation so incredibly frustrating. I mean, it's not like I don't realize what's happening. When I'm standing there, and my hand is just hovering over the twenties and the tens, I can see the customer. I can see the look on their face change from polite patience to annoyance, and then to this kind of weird concern, and my brain is screaming at me to just grab the change, hand it over, and say, 'Have a nice day.' But it's like... it's almost like the connection between my brain and my arm has just been completely severed for that moment. 

I'll try, I really do try so hard to just push my hand down into the drawer. I'll focus all my energy on it, but my body just simply won't respond. It's like I'm a statue, or like someone else has hit a pause button on my limbs, but my mind is still running at full speed. And with the scanner, the tapping thing... it's similar, but different. It's not that I'm frozen, but it's like this loop that I can't break out of. Tap, tap, tap on the edge of the counter. I'll look at the can of soup or whatever it is I'm supposed to be scanning, and I know I need to scan it, but my hand just keeps tapping. I try to force myself to stop, to just turn my wrist and point the laser, but the tapping just continues until it finally, eventually stops on its own.

Well, goodness no, absolutely nothing like this when I was younger. When I was a child, and even through my teenage years and into college—when I was earning my bachelor's degree, which took a lot of focus, I might add—I was completely typical. No tics, no strange habits, no getting stuck like a statue. I was always very coordinated and in control of myself. So if I had to give you an exact estimate, I would say that the voices and the more clearly out-of-place moments—you know, the freezing up and the tapping the scanner that I was just telling you about—have been happening for about the last three months. 

And three months... well, it might not sound like a terribly long time in the grand scheme of a 54-year-old's life, but let me tell you, Doctor, when you are standing at a checkout lane for eight hours a day, and you suddenly can't trust your own hands, or you're dealing with everything else going on, ninety days feels like an absolute eternity. Well, if someone actually came up and tried to move my arm... I don't know about that, because thankfully no one has tried to physically grab me at the store. And with the scanner, the tapping thing... it's similar, but different. It's not that I'm frozen, but it's like this loop that I can't break out of. Tap, tap, tap on the edge of the counter. I'll look at the can of soup or whatever it is I'm supposed to be scanning, and I know I need to scan it, but my hand just keeps tapping. I try to force myself to stop, to just turn my wrist and point the laser, but the tapping just continues until it finally, eventually stops on its own. \n\nIt's completely out of my control, which is exactly what I tried to explain to my manager when he pulled me into the office. I sat there in that little chair across from his desk, and I tried to tell him, 'Look, I'm not doing this on purpose to slow down the line or upset the customers.' But he just looked at his clipboard and said productivity was down and the complaints were piling up. He just didn't understand that I can't just snap out of it when I'm stuck like that. It's not a choice, Doctor. It really isn't. It's just my body refusing to do what it's supposed to do in that moment.\n\nDoctor: When you're tapping the scanner, do you feel any kind of tension, urge, or uncomfortable sensation building up before you start tapping, and does the tapping itself make that feeling go away?\n\nPatient: Well, that's an interesting question, Doctor, because you'd think there would be some kind of warning, wouldn't you? Like... like when you have to sneeze, you feel that tickle in your nose, or if you have a mosquito bite, you get that intense urge to scratch it to make it feel better. But with this... no. There is absolutely nothing like that at all. I don't feel any tension, no pressure, no uncomfortable sensation building up in my chest or my arm or anywhere else. \n\nI've actually thought about this quite a bit, especially after my manager handed me that write-up. I really tried to analyze exactly what was happening in my body right before the tapping starts. Like, just the other day, I was ringing up this older woman—she comes in every week, always buys the exact same brand of fancy canned cat food, the little ocean whitefish ones. Anyway, I was holding the scanner, looking right at the barcode on the tin, and I felt completely fine. Normal. My heart wasn't racing, I wasn't anxious, there was no... no urge or thought in my head telling me that I needed to tap the counter. One second I'm just holding the scanner, fully intending to scan the cat food, and the very next second, my wrist is just... going. Tap, tap, tap. \n\nAnd because there isn't any tension or weird feeling to begin with, the tapping certainly doesn't make anything go away. It doesn't bring me any relief whatsoever. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite! The tapping is what *causes* the tension, because once it starts, and I realize I'm doing it and I can't stop... well, *that's* when I start feeling stressed out. Because, you know, I'm 54 years old, I have a bachelor's degree, and I know exactly how bizarre it looks to the person standing across from me. I'm just standing there, watching my own hand tap a piece of plastic against the laminate counter, feeling completely disconnected from it, just... waiting for it to finish whatever it's doing so I can get back to work. So, no, there's no urge before, and no relief after. It just happens completely out of the blue.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been experiencing these tapping and freezing episodes? Did this start recently, or have you had similar kinds of involuntary movements or habits since you were younger—perhaps as a child or teenager?\n\nPatient: Well, goodness no, absolutely nothing like this when I was younger. When I was a child, and even through my teenage years and into college—when I was earning my bachelor's degree, which took a lot of focus, I might add—I was completely typical. No tics, no strange habits, no getting stuck like a statue. I was always very coordinated and in control of myself. So this is all entirely new to me, which is exactly why it’s been such a tremendous shock, and why it's been so incredibly disruptive to my life and my job. \n\nIf I really sit down and trace it back, try to put a firm timeline on it for you... it really wasn't that long ago at all. I remember we had this massive inventory weekend at the store, where the manager had us all working these grueling back-to-back shifts, and at first, I just chalked everything up to being terribly overworked and sleep-deprived. But that's really when things started shifting and becoming noticeable. So if I had to give you an exact estimate, I would say that the voices and the more clearly out-of-place moments—you know, the freezing up and the tapping the scanner that I was just telling you about—have been happening for about the last three months. \n\nAnd three months... well, it might not sound like a terribly long time in the grand scheme of a 54-year-old's life, but let me tell you, Doctor, when you are standing at a checkout lane for eight hours a day, and you suddenly can't trust your own hands, or you're dealing with everything else going on, ninety days feels like an absolute eternity. Because at first, it was just a little hesitation, just a tiny pause before handing over a receipt, but then it just escalated over these past three months into full-blown episodes where I'm just trapped in my own posture. And my manager, like I said, he just looks at the last three months of productivity metrics and thinks I'm suddenly a bad employee. He just looks at the numbers and the complaints from the last twelve weeks, but he doesn't see the whole picture of what's actually been happening to me since this all started... it's just been a really overwhelming three months.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned 'voices' just now when you were talking about the last three months. Can you tell me more about that? What exactly are you hearing, and how often does that happen?\n\nPatient: Oh, the voices. Yes, I suppose I did mention that, didn't I? It's... well, it's another one of those things that just makes the whole workday incredibly difficult to navigate, especially when I'm already dealing with the scanner tapping and the freezing up. It's just a lot to handle all at once. \n\nTo answer your question about what I'm hearing, it happens most days now. I'll just be standing there at my register, maybe bagging some produce or sorting out a customer's coupons, and I will hear what sounds exactly like a couple of people having a conversation just off to the side of me. It's usually right over my shoulder, close enough that you'd think they were standing right in my lane. \n\nSometimes, clear as day, I'll hear them calling my name from the stockroom. And our stockroom is all the way down past the dairy section, behind these heavy swinging double doors, so it's not exactly right next to the registers. But I'll hear my name being called out, and I'll actually turn around, completely expecting to see my manager or one of the overnight stock clerks leaning out of the doors trying to get my attention. \n\nOther times—and this is the part that really gets under my skin and makes me second-guess myself constantly—I'll be right in the middle of a transaction, ringing up groceries, and I'll hear these same voices commenting on what I'm doing. They'll say things like, 'He rang that up wrong,' or 'He missed the barcode on the cereal.' And I'll stop, and I'll check the monitor, and I'll check the receipt tape, because I take pride in my work, Doctor. I have a bachelor's degree, I know how to read a screen, so it's incredibly insulting to hear someone criticizing my scanning like I don't know what I'm doing. \n\nBut the truly baffling part, the thing that is just so incredibly frustrating about all of this, is that when I turn around to see who is whispering about my scanning, or who is shouting for me from the back... there is absolutely nobody there. Just empty space, or maybe a rack of chewing gum and batteries. And I'll look right at the customer standing in front of me, or the bagger at the end of the lane, and I'll ask them, 'Did you hear that? Did someone just say I double-scanned the bread?' And they just look at me with this blank expression. They just shake their heads. No one else hears a single word of it. It's just me, hearing these people talking, and it's happening almost every single day.\n\nDoctor: Besides the freezing episodes where your hand gets stuck, have you noticed any other times when your body feels unusually stiff or rigid, or when you hold positions that feel awkward for longer than normal—like if someone gently moved your arm into a position, it would just stay there?\n\nPatient: Well, if someone actually came up and tried to move my arm... I don't know about that, because thankfully no one has tried to physically grab me at the store. Customers are usually too busy looking at their phones or digging through their purses to reach across the counter and try to pose me like a mannequin. \n\nBut as far as the stiffness goes, or holding those awkward positions for way too long... yes, that's exactly what I've been trying to explain, and honestly, it’s the entire reason I came in to see you in the first place. I just keep getting stuck doing these things at the register that absolutely do not fit the moment. It’s like my body just completely loses the plot of what it’s supposed to be doing. \n\nFor instance, I'll be finishing up a cash transaction. The receipt prints out, the cash drawer pops open with that loud ding, and the customer is standing right there with their hand out, just waiting for their change. And I will just... freeze. My hand will be hovering right over the cash drawer, completely stiff, just suspended there in mid-air. I know I need to grab the five-dollar bills, I know the customer is literally staring at me waiting for their money, but I just hold that awkward position over the drawer for entirely too long. I can't seem to unstick myself. Or I get stuck doing the other thing I mentioned, tapping the scanner in a specific pattern against the counter when I should be ringing up the next item. \n\nNone of it fits what's actually happening around me. It makes no sense for a cashier to be doing those things. And, you know, it’s not just a minor inconvenience or a little quirk anymore. It actually got me written up last week. My manager pulled me into the back office—the cramped one with the tiny window that looks out over the self-checkout lanes—and handed me a formal warning printed on company letterhead. He said I was inexplicably halting transactions and exhibiting behavior that confused the customers. Can you imagine? I have a bachelor's degree, I am a professional, and I'm being handed a write-up like a teenager who doesn't know how to do his job. So, yes, the freezing over the drawer and getting stuck doing things that don't make sense... it’s threatening my livelihood, and that's exactly why I'm sitting here talking to you today.\n\nDoctor: When you're frozen with your hand stuck over the cash drawer, if your manager or a coworker gently pushed your arm down into the drawer and then let go, would your arm stay down in that position, or would it spring back up to where it was hovering?\n\nPatient: Well... see, that's the thing. Like I was trying to explain just a minute ago, nobody has actually ever done that. Nobody has ever reached out and grabbed my arm or pushed it down into the till. You have to picture the setup we have at the store to really understand why. I'm usually stationed on register four—that's one of the main lanes right by the front doors—and it's quite a narrow space. The customers are on the entirely opposite side of the scanner belt, and there's still a large plexiglass divider up from a few years ago, so they can't really reach me easily even if they wanted to. \n\nAnd as for my manager or my coworkers... well, the baggers are mostly just teenagers. Sixteen, seventeen years old at most. They're certainly not going to reach over and physically force a 54-year-old man's arm down into a cash drawer. They wouldn't dare. They just stand at the end of the bagging area looking completely bewildered when I get stuck. And my manager, like I mentioned, he doesn't come down to the floor to physically intervene or help me complete the transaction. He just watches from that little office window, taking notes so he can hand me another humiliating write-up later. People just don't manhandle you in a professional retail environment, especially not someone with a bachelor's degree who is just trying to do his job. \n\nSo, to answer your question about whether my arm would stay down there in the money or... or spring back up to where it was hovering... When I'm frozen there, it feels like I'm completely locked in that one specific spot, hovering right over the five-dollar bills, but since no one has ever violated my personal space to try and push my hand down, I simply couldn't tell you what my arm would do if they tried. It's always just me, stuck there all on my own, while the customer glares at me and the line backs up all the way into the seasonal aisle.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. Doctor, I... I feel like we are going in circles here. I really thought I just explained this. I don't mean to be difficult, but no, I do not feel like I need to obey them, because there is absolutely nothing to obey. They aren't giving me instructions. 

Like I was just saying, most days it’s just... it’s just this chatter. I'll be working, and I hear what sounds exactly like a couple of people talking just off to the side of me, usually over by the bagging area. Or, like I mentioned, sometimes it's them calling my name from the stockroom. And if you knew the layout of my store, the stockroom is a good fifty yards away through heavy metal double doors, so hearing someone yell my name from back there over the noise of the registers and the awful overhead music is incredibly distracting. But it's not a command! It's just my name. 

Or they say I rang something up wrong. That's the one that really gets me. They don't say, 'Hey, tap the scanner,' or 'Freeze right now.' They just say things like, 'He did that wrong,' or 'He charged them twice.' So if I stop what I'm doing, it's not because I'm obeying some invisible commander. I stop because I am terrified I actually made a mistake and I'm about to get fired! I'll whip around to see who is talking, fully expecting to see my manager standing there with his clipboard, but... there's nobody there. Just empty space. I'll look at the customer, and they're just staring at me, waiting for their receipt. No one else heard it. Not a single other person.
